name: TLV320AIC3100IRHBR
title: Low-power audio codec with stereo DAC, mono ADC, headphone driver and mono class-D speaker amplifier
summary: The TLV320AIC3100 is an I2C-controlled audio codec in a 5 mm × 5 mm 32-pin QFN: a 24-bit stereo DAC (95 dB SNR) and a mono ADC (91 dB SNR) at separate rates from 8 kHz to 192 kHz, each followed by selectable digital processing blocks with programmable biquad, IIR and FIR filters. On the analog side it has a microphone bias, a 0 to 59.5 dB microphone PGA with AGC, one differential and three single-ended inputs, a stereo headphone/line driver and a mono class-D speaker driver giving 2.5 W into 4 Ω from 5.5 V. An on-chip PLL, a beep generator, headset detection and an I2S/LJ/RJ/DSP/TDM serial port complete it.

circuits.title: Typical circuit configuration
circuits.description: A host processor drives the codec over I2C and the audio serial port (MCLK, BCLK, WCLK, DIN, DOUT), and also holds RESET and GPIO1. A 4 Ω speaker sits directly across the paired SPKP and SPKM outputs. A headset jack takes the two headphone outputs through 47 µF coupling capacitors; its microphone contact is biased from MICBIAS through 2.2 kΩ, watched by VOL/MICDET for headset and button detection, and coupled into MIC1RP by 0.1 µF. Two line sources enter MIC1LP and MIC1LM through 1 µF each. Every supply has a 0.1 µF capacitor beside a bulk one: 22 µF on each SPKVDD pin, 10 µF on HPVDD, AVDD, DVDD and IOVDD.
notes: SPKVDD runs from 2.7 V to 5.5 V, never below AVDD; 5 V is the example value.
All grounds are one net, joined on the board.

operation.text: A stereo DAC and a mono ADC, each with a fixed menu of digital processing blocks, sit between an audio serial port and the analog section: a microphone PGA with AGC, a programmable microphone bias, a stereo class-AB headphone/line driver and a mono class-D speaker driver. Everything is set through 8-bit registers over I2C; after a reset the part is in its default state with every block powered down.

The part is always an I2C slave at 7-bit address 001 1000 (0x18), standard or fast mode. Every writable register reads back. Leaving out the STOP after a write, or acknowledging after a read, steps on to the next register, so blocks of registers move in one transfer. A general-call response exists and is off at reset. Registers live on pages; writing register 0 of any page switches to another, and page 0 is selected after reset.

Bring up SPKVDD first, then IOVDD, then DVDD soon after it, then AVDD and HPVDD; power-down in the reverse order if the system wants it. The part tolerates other orders, but keeping digital activity apart from the analog and speaker rails avoids rare odd behaviour.

RESET held low for at least 10 ns, with IOVDD and DVDD present, puts the part in its default state; holding RESET low while DVDD rises is the suggested practice. Writing 1 to page 0 / register 1, bit D0 does the same in software. Internal memories take up to 1 ms after RESET rises to initialise; during that time the coefficient buffers are not touched and no block is powered up.

The fractional PLL takes 512 kHz to 20 MHz from MCLK, BCLK, GPIO1 or DIN and makes PLL_CLK = PLL_CLKIN × R × J.D / P. It is powered by page 0 / register 5, bit D7, and its clock is ready about 10 ms later. Simple dividers alone draw less power, so the PLL is for clocks that are not an integer multiple of the audio rates. When CODEC_CLKIN comes from the PLL, the PLL is powered up first and down last.

CODEC_CLKIN (MCLK, BCLK, GPIO1 or PLL_CLK, page 0 / register 4, D1-D0) is divided by NDAC and MDAC to the DAC processing and modulator clocks, then by DOSR to DAC_fS; NADC, MADC and AOSR do the same for the ADC. Dividers are powered up root first and powered down child first, and the NDAC/MDAC or NADC/MADC dividers stay on until the channel's power-down flag shows it has finished shutting down. With the ADC dividers off, the ADC clock comes from the DAC clocks. BCLK can be driven from a divider (1 to 128) of the DAC or ADC clocks, and a general-purpose clock can be sent out on GPIO1 or DOUT.
Debounce, power-up timers and interrupt pulses run from the internal 8.2 MHz oscillator divided by 8, or from MCLK through a divider (page 3 / register 16) set to give about 1 MHz.

MICBIAS supplies up to 4 mA at 2 V, 2.5 V or AVDD (page 1 / register 46); 2.5 V is the usual choice, though the best level depends on the microphone. MICBIAS off draws least current, and AVDD next least. The microphone PGA spans 0 dB to 59.5 dB in 0.5 dB steps with soft-stepping and resets to mute. Each input has a selectable series resistance of 10 kΩ, 20 kΩ or 40 kΩ that adds 6 dB, 0 dB or -6 dB to the programmed gain. A built-in second-order anti-alias filter gives 20 dB at 1 MHz, so the inputs need no external filtering.

The AGC holds the recorded level near a target of -5.5 dB to -24 dB below full scale by moving the PGA gain, judging level from the average of the absolute signal through a first-order low-pass (page 4 / registers 2 to 7). Attack and decay times, a maximum gain of 0 dB to 59.5 dB, a noise threshold of -30 dB to -90 dB with its own debounce, and hysteresis are all programmable. Below the noise threshold the gain falls to 0 dB in 0.5 dB steps. With the threshold at -70, -80 or -90 dB the maximum gain must be at least 11.5, 21.5 or 31.5 dB. The AGC works only with the microphone routed to the ADC and is set up before the ADC is powered.

A delta-sigma modulator with AOSR up to 128 feeds a decimation filter chosen through the processing block (filter A to 48 kHz or 96 kHz at AOSR 64, B to 96 kHz, C for 192 kHz at AOSR 32). The ADC's output rate reaches 192 kHz. ADC power is page 0 / register 81, bit D7, and its status reads at page 0 / register 36, bit D6. The mono result is sent in both the left and right slots of the serial port. ADC fine and coarse digital volume run -12 dB to 20 dB in 0.5 dB steps.

One digital microphone can replace the analog path: GPIO1 sends ADC_MOD_CLK to it (page 0 / register 51, D5-D2 = 1010), its one-bit output comes in on DIN, and data is taken on the rising clock edge. The analog ADC section can then be powered down, and AOSR sets the decimation to suit the microphone.

With the ADC not recording, page 0 / register 102, bit D7 turns it into a 24-bit dc meter (2.22 format, read from page 0 / registers 104 to 106 after latching with page 0 / register 103, bit D6). Mode A averages over a length of 1 to 20; mode B uses a first-order IIR whose bandwidth D sets. The averager can be reset every 2^R modulator clocks, with D less than R.

Each DAC channel has a processing block, an interpolation filter (A to 48 kHz, B to 96 kHz, C for 192 kHz), a multibit delta-sigma modulator and an analog filter that rebuilds the waveform, with DOSR from 1 to 1024 and rates from 8 kHz to 192 kHz. Digital volume runs from 24 dB to -63.5 dB in 0.5 dB steps per channel (page 0 / registers 65 and 66), soft-stepped at 0.125 dB per sample or half that rate. With soft-stepping on, CODEC_CLKIN stays running until the DAC power-up flag clears.

Setting page 0 / register 116, bit D7 hands DAC volume to the VOL/MICDET pin: a 7-bit SAR reads the pin and overwrites the digital volume, 18 dB at 0 V down to mute, with the applied value readable at page 0 / register 117. The pin voltage must stay at or below AVDD/2, so R1 above the potentiometer is never 0 Ω.

The DRC watches the DAC volume output after a high-pass and low-pass energy estimate (default corners 0.00166 × and 0.00033 × DAC_fS) and pulls gain down above a threshold of -3 dBFS to -24 dBFS in 3 dB steps, with 0 dB to 3 dB of hysteresis. Attack is programmable from 4 dB to 1.2207e-5 dB per sample and decay from 1.5625e-3 dB to 4.7683e-7 dB per sample. Suggested settings: threshold -24 dB, hysteresis 3 dB, hold 0, attack 1.9531e-4 dB per sample, decay 2.4414e-5 dB per sample.

With the jack wired to HPL, HPR, MICBIAS and VOL/MICDET, the part detects plug insertion and removal (debounce 32 ms to 512 ms) and button presses (8 ms to 32 ms), tells stereo headphones from a cellular headset, and flags each event in sticky and live status bits or as an interrupt. It needs AVDD and adds under 20 µA.

Two interrupts, INT1 and INT2, can each be raised by headset or button events, DRC threshold, AGC noise, driver overcurrent, processing overflow or dc-measurement data, and sent out on GPIO1 or DOUT as one pulse or a pulse train that runs until the flag registers are read.

Processing block PRB_P25 includes a sine generator for key clicks: a 16-bit sine and cosine coefficient set the frequency up to fS/2, a 24-bit length sets the burst in samples (up to 16 777 215), and left and right levels run 2 dB to -61 dB in 1 dB steps. The reset setting is about 1 kHz for five cycles at 48 kHz. CODEC_CLKIN, DAC, analog volume and output driver must all be on for the beep to sound.

While the DAC runs its coefficients are locked unless adaptive mode (page 8 / register 1, bit D2) is on; then two buffers hold coefficients and writes go to the idle one, swapped at the next sample by bit D0, with bit D1 showing the buffer in use. Without adaptive mode, the safe sequence is: ramp the volume down, power the channel down, write, power up, wait 20 ms and ramp back (DAC waits 20 ms at 48 kHz or 25 ms at 32 kHz; ADC 8 ms or 10 ms).

Each of the headphone and speaker paths has its own analog attenuator from 0 dB to -78 dB with mute, mostly in 0.5 dB steps and soft-stepped, usable with the ADC and DAC off. DAC_L and DAC_R are routed to it by page 1 / register 35.

HPL and HPR deliver up to 30 mW per channel into 16 Ω at 3.3 V, single-ended through a dc-blocking capacitor, and also drive 32 Ω and 10 kΩ without changes. A lower-power line-out mode is set by page 1 / register 44, D2-D1 = 11. Output common mode is 1.35 V, 1.5 V, 1.65 V or 1.8 V and is set no higher than AVDD/2. Gain is 0 dB to 9 dB in 1 dB steps. Short-circuit protection is always on and either limits current (default) or shuts the driver down; a shut-down driver is restarted by a full reset or by its own power-stage reset bit (page 1 / register 31, D7 for HPL, D6 for HPR). More than three restarts into a standing fault risks overheating.

The mono class-D driver drives a 4 Ω differential load from SPKVDD of 2.7 V to 5.5 V, which may be the battery, with spikes kept under 6 V; it gives 1 W into 4 Ω at 3.6 V and 2.5 W at 5.5 V. Gain is 6 dB to 24 dB in 6 dB steps. An output short always shuts it down (no current limit), and it is restarted by reset or by page 1 / register 32, bit D7. Thermal protection stops switching while the die is hot and resumes when it cools; the flag is page 0 / register 3, bit D1.
After reset and set-up, each output stage is powered by its own bit and soft-starts, so all of them can be turned on together.

The port runs I2S, left-justified, right-justified, DSP and TDM formats, MSB first, in 16, 20, 24 or 32 bits, with WCLK and BCLK each independently master or slave. A data offset in bit clocks, BCLK inversion and a high-impedance DOUT between slots let several devices share one bus; a bus keeper can hold DOUT's last value. Clocks the part generates run only while a converter is on unless set to run always. In right- and left-justified and DSP modes the frame holds at least twice the word length in bit clocks; in I2S each half holds at least one word. A second set of WCLK, BCLK, DIN and DOUT can be taken through GPIO1 and DOUT to talk to a second processor, one at a time.

Every block is off after reset and is powered individually; settings survive power-down while supplies stay up. The choice of processing block sets most of the digital power, from resource class 2 to 12.
Speaker supplies come up first, then digital, then analog, each settled before the next. Decoupling capacitors sit close to each supply pin to keep the rails steady and avoid pops.

The thermal pad goes to the analog output-driver ground through several vias. Analog and digital grounds are kept separate. Decoupling capacitors sit as close as possible to the supply pins. Differential audio signals are routed as pairs where possible.
